questions.q: A fraud model always predicts "not fraud" and scores 99% accuracy on a dataset where 1% of transactions are fraud. What does this reveal about accuracy?
options: Accuracy is always the best metric regardless of class balance
Accuracy can be dangerously misleading on imbalanced data, since ignoring the minority class entirely still scores well
99% accuracy proves the model is catching most fraud
This situation is impossible in practice
questions.explain: On an imbalanced dataset, a model that ignores the input and always predicts the majority class can score deceptively high accuracy while being useless at its actual job.

questions.q: In the scikit-learn confusion matrix example, what does it mean that 13 of 16 true versicolor examples were predicted as virginica?
options: The model is perfect on versicolor
The model systematically confuses versicolor for virginica, which a single accuracy number would hide
Virginica and versicolor are the same class
The model never predicts virginica
questions.explain: The confusion matrix shows exactly which classes get mixed up with which — here, most true versicolor examples were misclassified as virginica, a pattern that an overall accuracy score alone would not reveal.

options: Of everything predicted positive, how much actually was positive
Of everything that was actually positive, how much the model correctly caught
The total number of predictions made
How fast the model runs inference
questions.explain: Recall is true positives divided by (true positives + false negatives) — it measures how much of the real positive class the model actually catches.

questions.q: Why do precision and recall typically trade off against each other?
options: They don't trade off; they always move together
A model that flags more cases as positive to catch more real positives (raising recall) also tends to raise false alarms (lowering precision), and vice versa
Precision only applies to regression problems
Recall can only be computed after precision is already known
questions.explain: Flagging everything as positive maximizes recall (you catch every real case) but tanks precision (lots of false alarms); flagging only the most obvious cases raises precision but misses more real cases, lowering recall.

questions.q: Which metrics are appropriate for a regression problem (predicting a continuous number), rather than classification?
options: Precision and recall
Accuracy and F1 score
A confusion matrix
MAE, RMSE, and R-squared
questions.explain: Regression has no discrete class to be right or wrong about, so it uses error-magnitude metrics like MAE and RMSE, and R-squared for variance explained, instead of classification metrics.
